claims.claim: Exposure is the total amount of light the sensor records for one frame; too little light underexposes (dark) and too much overexposes (washed out).
Aperture, shutter speed, and ISO form the exposure triangle and together determine exposure; changing one affects the balance and usually must be compensated by another.

Aperture is the lens opening, measured in f-stops; a wide aperture (low f-number) lets in more light and gives shallow depth of field, and a narrow aperture (high f-number) lets in less light and gives deeper depth of field.

The f-number is the focal length divided by the diameter of the entrance pupil, so a larger f-number denotes a smaller opening; the full-stop scale (f/1, 1.4, 2, 2.8, 4, 5.6, 8, 11, 16, 22) steps by the square root of two, each step halving or doubling the light.
Shutter speed is how long the sensor is exposed; fast shutter speeds freeze motion and slow shutter speeds blur it.
ISO is the sensor's sensitivity/amplification; higher ISO brightens the image from the same light but increases noise and can reduce image quality.

A stop is a doubling or halving of the light in an exposure, and each control is calibrated in stops so they can be traded against one another (e.g. going from 1/500 s to 1/250 s adds one stop; the full f-stop scale changes light by one stop per step).

RAW files store the sensor's full unprocessed capture and give greater latitude to adjust exposure and white balance in post-processing without degrading the image; JPEG files are compressed and processed in-camera, smaller and ready to use but with less editing flexibility.

Worked example: from f/8, 1/250 s, ISO 100, opening to f/2.8 is three stops brighter (f/8 -> f/5.6 -> f/4 -> f/2.8); shortening the shutter three stops to 1/2000 s (1/250 -> 1/500 -> 1/1000 -> 1/2000) restores the same exposure value.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether ISO physically changes sensor 'sensitivity' or amplifies the captured signal.
positions: Introductory texts describe ISO as sensor sensitivity to light.
Engineering descriptions frame ISO as amplification/gain applied to the captured signal.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses 'how strongly the signal is amplified' as the primary framing and mentions sensitivity as the conventional term, avoiding an overclaim while matching the OER sources; the practical fact (higher ISO = brighter file + more noise) is identical either way.

Supports: the exposure-triangle framing (shutter speed, aperture, ISO working together for correct exposure); shutter speed measured in fractions of a second, fast freezes / slow blurs motion; aperture measured in f-stops, wide aperture (low f-stop) = more light + shallow depth of field, narrow (high f-stop) = less light + deep depth of field; ISO = sensitivity, low ISO = cleaner, high ISO = brighter in low light but more noise; changing one setting must be compensated by another; RAW keeps all sensor data with greater post-processing flexibility for exposure and white balance, JPEG is compressed with limited editing flexibility. sourceRecords.title: F-number
sourceRecords.notes: Encyclopedia reference read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19, used only to corroborate the well-established, evergreen optics that underlie the stop concept: the f-number equals focal length divided by entrance-pupil diameter (so a larger number is a smaller opening); the standard full-stop scale f/1, 1.4, 2, 2.8, 4, 5.6, 8, 11, 16, 22 steps by the square root of two because light depends on the square of the aperture diameter, so each step halves or doubles the light (one stop); and a lower f-number gives a larger aperture, more light, and shallower depth of field. This mathematics was independently re-derived and checked in Bash. Treated as reference only; no wording reproduced.
